concepts: Plane in intercept form, distance from the origin and locus
questions.question: A variable plane is at a constant distance $p$ from the origin and meets the coordinate axes in points $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Through these points, planes are drawn parallel to the coordinate planes. Find the locus of their point of intersection.
questions.key_idea: The three parallel planes meet at $(a,b,c)$, the intercepts themselves, so the intercept relation is already the locus.
solution: Let the plane be $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}+\frac{z}{c}=1$, where $a,b,c$ are its intercepts on the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes, so $A(a,0,0)$, $B(0,b,0)$, $C(0,0,c)$.
Its distance from the origin is $p$: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}+\frac{1}{c^2}}}=p$.
The planes through $A$, $B$, $C$ parallel to the coordinate planes are $x=a$, $y=b$, $z=c$.
Their point of intersection is $(a,b,c)$; call it $(x,y,z)$, so $a=x$, $b=y$, $c=z$.
Substituting in the relation above, the locus is $\frac{1}{x^2}+\frac{1}{y^2}+\frac{1}{z^2}=\frac{1}{p^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the normal form $lx+my+nz=p$ with direction cosines, so the intercepts are $p/l$, $p/m$, $p/n$.
solution: A plane at distance $p$ from the origin has the normal form $lx+my+nz=p$, where $l,m,n$ are the direction cosines of the perpendicular from the origin, so $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
Its intercepts are $a=\frac{p}{l}$, $b=\frac{p}{m}$, $c=\frac{p}{n}$, hence the intersection point of the three parallel planes is $(x,y,z)=\left(\frac pl,\frac pm,\frac pn\right)$.

useful_results: A plane with intercepts $a,b,c$ is at distance $d$ from the origin where $\frac{1}{d^2}=\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}+\frac{1}{c^2}$; conversely, the reciprocal squares of the intercepts add to $\frac1{d^2}$.
The point $(a,b,c)$ made from the intercepts is the vertex of the box opposite to the origin; any condition on the intercepts becomes the locus of this point by renaming $a,b,c$ as $x,y,z$.

If instead the plane passes through a fixed point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\frac{\alpha}{a}+\frac{\beta}{b}+\frac{\gamma}{c}=1$ and the same renaming gives the locus $\frac{\alpha}{x}+\frac{\beta}{y}+\frac{\gamma}{z}=1$.

concepts: Line and plane in 3D: intersection and distance measured along a direction
questions.question: Let $\Pi: x+y-z-4=0$ be the equation of a plane and $A$ be the point with position vector $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$. $L$ is a line which passes through the point $(1,2,3)$ with direction ratios $3,-1$ and $4$. If the distance of the point $A$ from the line $L$ measured parallel to the plane $\Pi$ is $d_1$ and the distance of the point $A$ from the plane $\Pi$ measured parallel to the line $L$ is $d_2$, then find the value of $\sqrt{d_1^2-d_2^2}$.
questions.key_idea: Measured parallel to the plane means $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec{n}=0$ for $B$ on $L$; measured parallel to the line means moving from $A$ along $L$'s direction until the plane is hit.
solution: $L:\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{4}=r$, $A=(1,2,-3)$; the normal of the plane is $\vec n=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, and at $A$ the value of $x+y-z$ is $6\neq4$.
$\vec{AB}$ is parallel to the plane, so $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec n=0$: $3r-r-4r-6=0$, i.e. $2r=-6$ and $r=-3$.
For $d_2$: the line through $A(1,2,-3)$ with direction ratios $3,-1,4$ is $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z+3}{4}=\lambda$, i.e. $(3\lambda+1,\,2-\lambda,\,4\lambda-3)$.
The point on the plane is $(4,1,1)$, and its distance from $A$ is $\sqrt{9+1+16}=\sqrt{26}$, so $d_2^2=26$.
useful_results: Distance of $P$ from the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ measured along a direction $\vec v$ is $\frac{\left|\vec n\cdot\vec P-k\right|\,\left|\vec v\right|}{\left|\vec n\cdot\vec v\right|}$ (equal to the perpendicular distance divided by $\cos$ of the angle between $\vec v$ and $\vec n$). Here $\frac{2\sqrt{26}}{2}=\sqrt{26}$.
To move from a point $A$ to a line $L$ parallel to a plane, impose $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec n=0$ on the general point $B$ of $L$; this is valid whenever $L$ is not parallel to the plane.
Both measured distances are always at least the corresponding shortest (perpendicular) distances, with equality only when the direction coincides with the perpendicular.

concepts: Plane in intercept form and distance from a plane (point equidistant from faces of a tetrahedron)
questions.question: The position vectors of the four angular points of a tetrahedron $OABC$ are $(0,0,0)$; $(0,0,2)$; $(0,4,0)$ and $(6,0,0)$ respectively. A point $P$ inside the tetrahedron is at the same distance $r$ from the four plane faces of the tetrahedron. Find the value of $r$.
questions.key_idea: Three faces lie on the coordinate planes, so the equidistant point is $(r,r,r)$; its distance from face $ABC$ then gives an equation in $r$ (reject the root that puts $P$ outside).
solution: The faces $OAB$, $OAC$, $OBC$ lie in the coordinate planes $x=0$, $y=0$, $z=0$, so a point inside at distance $r$ from all three has coordinates $P=(r,r,r)$.
The face $ABC$ has intercepts $6,4,2$, so its plane is $\frac{x}{6}+\frac{y}{4}+\frac{z}{2}=1$.
Distance of $P$ from it: $r=\frac{\left|\frac r6+\frac r4+\frac r2-1\right|}{\sqrt{\frac1{6^2}+\frac1{4^2}+\frac1{2^2}}}$.
Here $\frac r6+\frac r4+\frac r2-1=\frac{11r-12}{12}$ and $\sqrt{\frac1{36}+\frac1{16}+\frac14}=\frac{7}{12}$, so $7r=\pm(11r-12)$.
$P$ lies inside only if $\frac{11r}{12}<1$, i.e. $r<\frac{12}{11}$; so $r=3$ is not acceptable (the point lies beyond face $ABC$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Inradius of a tetrahedron: $r=\frac{3V}{S}$, volume divided by total surface area (split the volume into four pyramids with apex $P$).
solution: Joining $P$ to the four vertices splits the tetrahedron into four pyramids with apex $P$, each of height $r$ over a face, so $V=\frac13 r\,(S_1+S_2+S_3+S_4)$, i.e. $r=\frac{3V}{S}$.
Face $ABC$: $\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}$ with $\vec{AB}=(0,4,-2)$, $\vec{AC}=(6,0,-2)$ is $(-8,-12,-24)$, magnitude $\sqrt{64+144+576}=28$, so the area is $14$.

useful_results: Inradius of any tetrahedron: $r=\frac{3V}{S}$, where $S$ is the total surface area; the incentre exists inside and is unique.
For a tetrahedron with mutually perpendicular edges $a,b,c$ at one vertex, $r=\frac{abc}{ab+bc+ca+\sqrt{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}}$ (here $\frac{48}{44+28}=\frac23$).
The area of the slant face $ABC$ is $\frac12\sqrt{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}$ (here $14$), the square root of the sum of squares of the three right-angled face areas.

When an equation $|\cdot|=\pm$ gives two roots, test which one keeps the point on the correct side of the faces (inside means each face's linear expression has the same sign as at the opposite vertex).

concepts: Line in 3D: foot of perpendicular and equation of lines through a point
questions.question: The line $\frac{x+6}{5}=\frac{y+10}{3}=\frac{z+14}{8}$ is the hypotenuse of an isosceles right angled triangle whose opposite vertex is $(7,2,4)$. Find the equation of the remaining sides.
questions.key_idea: In an isosceles right triangle the foot $P$ of the perpendicular from the right-angle vertex bisects the hypotenuse, so $PA=PC=BP$.
solution: Let $B=(7,2,4)$ be the right-angle vertex and $A$, $C$ the ends of the hypotenuse on the line; let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$, so $P=(5k-6,\,3k-10,\,8k-14)$.
In the isosceles right triangle $P$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $PA=PC=BP=\frac{\sqrt{98}}{2}$.
Moving $\frac{\sqrt{98}}{2}$ along the unit vector $\frac{(5,3,8)}{\sqrt{98}}$ on either side of $P$: $A,C=\left(\frac{13}{2}\pm\frac52,\,-\frac52\pm\frac32,\,6\pm4\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The legs make $45^\circ$ with the hypotenuse, so their directions are $\hat{p}\pm\hat{u}$, with $\hat p$ the unit vector along $BP$ and $\hat u$ along the hypotenuse.
solution: The hypotenuse has unit direction $\hat u=\frac{(5,3,8)}{\sqrt{98}}$. Foot of the perpendicular: $k=\frac52$ as before, so $\vec{BP}=\left(-\frac12,-\frac92,2\right)$ and $\hat p=\frac{(-1,-9,4)}{\sqrt{98}}$ is the unit vector from $B$ to $P$.
At $B$ each leg makes $45^\circ$ with $BP$ (angle $PBA=45^\circ$ since $PA=PB$), and $\hat p\perp\hat u$, so the unit vectors along $BA$ and $BC$ are $\frac{\hat p\pm\hat u}{\sqrt2}$.
Check: $(2,-3,6)\cdot(3,6,2)=6-18+12=0$, as it must be for a right angle at $B$. Same two lines.

useful_results: In an isosceles right triangle, the median to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse and is also the altitude: $PA=PB=PC$ for the foot $P$.

The legs through $B$ are directed along $\hat p\pm\hat u$ ($\hat p$ the unit vector from $B$ to the foot, $\hat u$ the unit direction of the hypotenuse); they are automatically perpendicular because $|\hat p|=|\hat u|=1$ and $\hat p\perp\hat u$.

Foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to a line with direction $\vec d$ through $Q$: take $P=Q+t\vec d$ with $t=\frac{\vec{QB}\cdot\vec d}{\left|\vec d\right|^2}$. Here $t=\frac{(13,12,18)\cdot(5,3,8)}{98}=\frac{245}{98}=\frac52$ for $Q=(-6,-10,-14)$.

concepts: Plane in intercept form and distance from origin
AM-GM inequality
questions.question: Consider a plane passing through three points $A(a,0,0)$, $B(0,b,0)$, $C(0,0,c)$ with $a>0,b>0,c>0$. Let $d$ be the distance between the origin $O$ and the plane and $m$ be the distance between the origin $O$ and the point $M(a,b,c)$. If $a,b,c$ vary in the range of any positive numbers, then find the minimum value of $\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^2$.
questions.key_idea: $\frac1{d^2}=\sum\frac1{a^2}$ and $m^2=\sum a^2$, so the ratio is $(\sum a^2)(\sum \frac1{a^2})$ and AM-GM applies.
solution: The plane is $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$, so $d=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}}}$, i.e. $\frac1{d^2}=\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}$.
Apply AM-GM to the last six terms: their mean is at least $(1)^{1/6}$, because the product of the six terms is $1$.
Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the vectors $(a,b,c)$ and $\left(\frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c\right)$: the product is at least $\left(a\cdot\frac1a+b\cdot\frac1b+c\cdot\frac1c\right)^2=3^2=9$.
Equality needs $(a,b,c)\parallel\left(\frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c\right)$, i.e. $a^2=b^2=c^2$, attainable at $a=b=c$ (for example $a=b=c=1$ gives $3\cdot3=9$).

useful_results: For positive $x_1,\dots,x_n$: $(x_1+\dots+x_n)\left(\frac1{x_1}+\dots+\frac1{x_n}\right)\ge n^2$, with equality iff all $x_i$ are equal (AM-HM or Cauchy-Schwarz). With $x_i=a_i^2$ and $n=3$ this gives $9$.

Distance of the plane $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ from the origin: $d=\left(\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\right)^{-1/2}$, and $d\le\frac{m}{3}$ always, where $m=OM$ with $M=(a,b,c)$ (here $d\le\frac m3$ is the same inequality).
The expression is unchanged by scaling $(a,b,c)\to(ta,tb,tc)$, so the minimum is on the whole ray $a=b=c$, not a single point.

concepts: Volume of a tetrahedron, face areas and altitudes
AM-HM inequality
questions.question: Let $A_1,A_2,A_3,A_4$ be the areas of the triangular faces of a tetrahedron, and $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$ be the corresponding altitudes of the tetrahedron. If the volume of the tetrahedron is $5$ cubic units, then find the minimum value of $(A_1+A_2+A_3+A_4)(h_1+h_2+h_3+h_4)$ (in cubic units).
questions.key_idea: Since $V=\frac13A_ih_i$ for every face, $h_i=\frac{3V}{A_i}$, which turns the product into $3V(\sum A_i)(\sum\frac1{A_i})$ and AM-HM gives the bound.
solution: So $(A_1+A_2+A_3+A_4)\left(\frac1{A_1}+\frac1{A_2}+\frac1{A_3}+\frac1{A_4}\right)\ge16$, with equality when all faces have equal area (for example a regular tetrahedron).
The minimum of the product is $3V\cdot16=48V=48\cdot5=240$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $A_ih_i=3V$ for every face, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to $\sqrt{A_i}$ and $\sqrt{h_i}$ directly, with no need to invert the areas.
solution: Every face satisfies $A_ih_i=3V$, so $\sqrt{A_ih_i}=\sqrt{3V}$ for each $i=1,2,3,4$.
Equality needs $A_i\propto h_i$ together with $A_ih_i$ constant, i.e. all $A_i$ equal, which occurs for a regular tetrahedron of volume $5$, so $240$ is attained and is the minimum.

useful_results: For any tetrahedron $h_i=\frac{3V}{A_i}$, hence $A_ih_i=3V$ for all four faces, and $\sum\frac{1}{h_i}=\frac{1}{3V}\sum A_i$.
$(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{x_i}\right)\ge n^2$ for positive $x_i$ (equality iff all equal): for $n=4$ it gives $16$.
The bound $(\sum A_i)(\sum h_i)\ge48V$ holds for every tetrahedron; equality iff all four faces have the same area (which does not force the tetrahedron to be regular; a disphenoid also works).

concepts: Vector triple product and rotation of a vector in a plane
questions.question: The vector $\vec{OP}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ turns through a right angle, passing through the positive $x$-axis on the way. Find the vector in its new position.
questions.key_idea: The new vector lies in the plane of $\vec{OP}$ and $\hat i$, is perpendicular to $\vec{OP}$ and has the same length; $(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}$ gives that direction.
solution: Let the new vector be $\vec{OP'}$; $\left|\vec{OP}\right|=3$ and $\left|\vec{OP'}\right|=3$, and $\vec{OP'}\perp\vec{OP}$ (turned through a right angle).
It passes through the positive $x$-axis on the way, so $\vec{OP}$, $\hat i$ and $\vec{OP'}$ are coplanar.

The vector $(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}$ lies in this plane and is perpendicular to $\vec{OP}$, so $\vec{OP'}=\left|\vec{OP}\right|\frac{(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}}{\left|(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}\right|}$.
$\vec{OP}\times\hat i=(0,2,-2)$, and $(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}=8\hat i-2\hat j-2\hat k$.
So $\vec{OP'}=\frac{4}{\sqrt2}\hat i-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat j-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat k$; its $\hat i$ component is positive, so it is the sense of turning towards (and past) the $x$-axis, as required.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec{OP'}=x\hat i+y\,\vec{OP}$ (coplanar), then impose perpendicularity, length $3$ and the sense of rotation.
solution: Coplanarity with $\vec{OP}$ and $\hat i$ lets us write $\vec{OP'}=x\hat i+y\vec{OP}$, with $\hat i\cdot\vec{OP}=1$ and $\left|\vec{OP}\right|^2=9$.
The $\hat i$ component of $\vec{OP'}$ is $x+y=-8y$; the vector turns towards $\hat i$ and beyond it, so this must be positive: $y=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}$, $x=\frac{9}{2\sqrt2}$.
$\vec{OP'}=\frac{9}{2\sqrt2}\hat i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\left(\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\right)=\frac{8\hat i-2\hat j-2\hat k}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{4}{\sqrt2}\hat i-\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j-\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$.

useful_results: For nonzero $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ (not parallel): $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a=\left|\vec a\right|^2\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a$, the component of $\vec b$ perpendicular to $\vec a$ scaled by $\left|\vec a\right|^2$. Here $9\hat i-\vec{OP}=(8,-2,-2)$.

Rotating $\vec a$ by $90^\circ$ in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ towards $\vec b$ gives $\left|\vec a\right|\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a}{\left|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a\right|}$; towards the opposite side use the negative.
A vector at a right angle to $\vec a$ in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ has the form $\vec b-\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec a\right|^2}\vec a$ up to scale.

concepts: Dot product, cross product and angle between vectors
questions.question: If $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are two vectors such that $\left|\vec a\right|=1$, $\left|\vec b\right|=4$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$, and $\vec c=(2\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$, then find the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$.
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so the cross term vanishes in both $\left|\vec c\right|^2$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
solution: From $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec b\right|\cos\theta$: $2=1\cdot4\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta=\frac12$ and $\theta=60^\circ$ between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.
$\left|\vec c\right|^2=\left|2\vec a\times\vec b\right|^2+9\left|\vec b\right|^2-2\cdot3\,\vec b\cdot(2\vec a\times\vec b)$, and the last term is $0$ because $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec b\cdot(2\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b\cdot\vec b=0-3\cdot16=-48$.
With $\phi$ the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$: $4\cdot8\sqrt3\cos\phi=-48$, so $\cos\phi=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose coordinates: $\vec a=(1,0,0)$ and $\vec b=(2,2\sqrt3,0)$ fit the given lengths and dot product; compute $\vec c$ outright.
solution: Take $\vec a=(1,0,0)$ and $\vec b=(2,2\sqrt3,0)$: $\left|\vec b\right|^2=4+12=16$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$, as required.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so $\left|\vec u\times\vec b+\lambda\vec b\right|^2=\left|\vec u\times\vec b\right|^2+\lambda^2\left|\vec b\right|^2$ for any $\vec u$.
Lagrange's identity: $\left|\vec a\times\vec b\right|^2=\left|\vec a\right|^2\left|\vec b\right|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ (here $16-4=12$).
Since only $\left|\vec a\right|,\left|\vec b\right|$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ are given, the answer cannot depend on the choice of axes; a convenient coordinate model is always valid.

concepts: Distance of a point from a line and a plane, volume of a tetrahedron, shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The position vectors of the four angular points of a tetrahedron are: $A\left(\hat{j}+2\hat{k}\right)$; $B\left(3\hat{i}+\hat{k}\right)$; $C\left(4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+6\hat{k}\right)$ and $D\left(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}\right)$. Find: (i) the perpendicular distance from $A$ to the line $BC$. (ii) the volume of the tetrahedron $ABCD$. (iii) the perpendicular distance from $D$ to the plane $ABC$. (iv) the shortest distance between the lines $AB$ and $CD$.
questions.key_idea: Four standard formulas on the same four points: foot of perpendicular, $\frac16|[\,]|$, plane distance, and $\frac{|\vec{AC}\cdot(\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD})|}{|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}|}$.
solution: For the foot of the perpendicular $\vec{AP}\cdot\vec{BC}=0$: $3+\lambda+9\lambda-3+25\lambda-5=0$, so $35\lambda=5$ and $\lambda=\frac17$.
(iii) Normal to plane $ABC$: $\vec{AB}\times\vec{BC}=(-2,-16,10)\parallel(1,8,-5)$; plane through $A$: $x+8y-5z=-2$, i.e. $x+8y-5z+2=0$.
questions.correction_note: Part (iii): the PDF used $|2+24-10|=16$ and got $\frac{16}{3\sqrt{10}}=\frac{8}{15}\sqrt{10}$; the plane is $x+8y-5z+2=0$ so the numerator is $|2+24-10+2|=18$, giving $\frac{18}{3\sqrt{10}}=\frac35\sqrt{10}$ (the printed answer is right, the working was not). Smaller slips: in (i) the PDF wrote $\vec{AP}$ as $(3+\lambda,3\lambda,1+5\lambda)$, which is the point $P$ (the dot product it then evaluates uses the correct $\vec{AP}$); in (iv) it wrote the cross product first as $4\hat i+4\hat j-2\hat k$ and then as $(4,14,-2)$, and $\sqrt{120}$ in place of $\sqrt{216}$ in one line.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the cross-product and volume relations: $d(A,BC)=\frac{|\vec{AB}\times\vec{BC}|}{|\vec{BC}|}$, $h=\frac{3V}{\text{Area}}$ and $d_{AB,CD}=\frac{6V}{|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}|}$.
solution: All four values agree with the first method.

useful_results: Distance from a point $A$ to the line through $B$ with direction $\vec u$: $\frac{\left|\vec{BA}\times\vec u\right|}{\left|\vec u\right|}$ (no foot of the perpendicular needed).
Height of $D$ above plane $ABC$ equals $\frac{3V}{\text{Area}(ABC)}=\frac{\left|\vec{AD}\cdot(\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC})\right|}{\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}\right|}$.

For opposite edges $AB$ and $CD$ of a tetrahedron with shortest distance $d$: $V=\frac16\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}\right|d$, so $d=\frac{6V}{\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}\right|}$. Here $\frac{36}{6\sqrt6}=\sqrt6$.
When the plane equation is written $x+8y-5z+2=0$, put in the constant term with its sign before substituting the point; check by substituting the three known points into the equation.

concepts: Scalar triple product and its determinant form
questions.question: If $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$; $\vec b=b_1\hat i+b_2\hat j+b_3\hat k$ and $\vec c=c_1\hat i+c_2\hat j+c_3\hat k$, then show that the value of the scalar triple product $\left[n\vec a+\vec b\quad n\vec b+\vec c\quad n\vec c+\vec a\right]$ is $(n^3+1)\left|\begin{matrix}\vec a\cdot\hat i&\vec a\cdot\hat j&\vec a\cdot\hat k\\ \vec b\cdot\hat i&\vec b\cdot\hat j&\vec b\cdot\hat k\\ \vec c\cdot\hat i&\vec c\cdot\hat j&\vec c\cdot\hat k\end{matrix}\right|$.
questions.answer: $\left[n\vec a+\vec b\quad n\vec b+\vec c\quad n\vec c+\vec a\right]=(n^3+1)\left[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c\right]$, which equals $(n^3+1)$ times the given determinant
questions.key_idea: Expanding by distributivity, every triple product with a repeated vector vanishes, leaving $n^3[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]+[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]$.
solution: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$ is the determinant of the components, and since $\vec a\cdot\hat i=a_1$, $\vec a\cdot\hat j=a_2$, $\vec a\cdot\hat k=a_3$, etc., this is exactly $\left|\begin{matrix}\vec a\cdot\hat i&\vec a\cdot\hat j&\vec a\cdot\hat k\\ \vec b\cdot\hat i&\vec b\cdot\hat j&\vec b\cdot\hat k\\ \vec c\cdot\hat i&\vec c\cdot\hat j&\vec c\cdot\hat k\end{matrix}\right|$.
Now $\left[n\vec a+\vec b\quad n\vec b+\vec c\quad n\vec c+\vec a\right]=\{(n\vec a+\vec b)\times(n\vec b+\vec c)\}\cdot(n\vec c+\vec a)$.
$(n\vec a+\vec b)\times(n\vec b+\vec c)=n^2(\vec a\times\vec b)+n(\vec a\times\vec c)+n(\vec b\times\vec b)+\vec b\times\vec c=n^2(\vec a\times\vec b)+n(\vec a\times\vec c)+\vec b\times\vec c$.
Dot with $n\vec c+\vec a$: terms $n^2(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot n\vec c=n^3[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ and $n^2(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a=0$.
Terms $n(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot n\vec c=0$ and $n(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot\vec a=0$ (a vector repeated in a triple product).
Terms $(\vec b\times\vec c)\cdot n\vec c=0$ and $(\vec b\times\vec c)\cdot\vec a=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
Adding: $\left[n\vec a+\vec b\quad n\vec b+\vec c\quad n\vec c+\vec a\right]=n^3[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]+[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=(n^3+1)[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
By the first step this is $(n^3+1)$ times the given determinant, as to be shown.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the three new vectors as rows of $(nI+P)$ times the matrix with rows $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, and use $\det(XY)=\det X\det Y$.
solution: Let $M$ be the $3\times3$ matrix with rows $\vec a$, $\vec b$, $\vec c$; then $\det M=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
The rows $n\vec a+\vec b$, $n\vec b+\vec c$, $\vec a+n\vec c$ form the matrix $XM$ with $X=\begin{pmatrix}n&1&0\\0&n&1\\1&0&n\end{pmatrix}$.
By $\det(XM)=\det X\cdot\det M$: $\left[n\vec a+\vec b\quad n\vec b+\vec c\quad n\vec c+\vec a\right]=(n^3+1)[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
Since $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ equals the determinant of the dot products with $\hat i,\hat j,\hat k$ (the components), the required result follows.

useful_results: A triple product with a repeated vector is $0$, and $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]=-[\vec b\ \vec a\ \vec c]$ (cyclic symmetry).

If $\vec u=X\cdot(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c)^T$ for a $3\times3$ coefficient matrix $X$, then $[\vec u_1\ \vec u_2\ \vec u_3]=\det X\,[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$; the triple product behaves like a determinant of coefficients.
For $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ in a cyclic pattern $p\vec a+q\vec b,\ p\vec b+q\vec c,\ p\vec c+q\vec a$ the factor is $p^3+q^3$ (here $p=n$, $q=1$; check $n=1$: factor $2$).
$[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ is another standard identity of this type.

concepts: Position vectors, parallelogram and area of a triangle using the cross product
questions.question: $ABCD$ is a tetrahedron with position vectors of its angular points $A(-5,22,5)$; $B(1,2,3)$; $C(4,3,2)$ and $D(-1,2,-3)$. If the area of the triangle $AEF$, where the quadrilaterals $ABDE$ and $ABCF$ are parallelograms, is $\sqrt S$, then find the value of $S$.
questions.key_idea: In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so $E$ and $F$ follow from midpoint equalities; then take half the cross product.
solution: Diagonals $AD$ and $BE$ bisect each other: midpoint of $AD=(-3,12,1)=\left(\frac{\alpha+1}{2},\frac{\beta+2}{2},\frac{\gamma+3}{2}\right)$.
Let $F=(a,b,c)$ with $ABCF$ a parallelogram: midpoint of $AC=\left(-\frac12,\frac{25}{2},\frac72\right)=\left(\frac{1+a}{2},\frac{2+b}{2},\frac{3+c}{2}\right)$.
Area of $\triangle AEF=\frac12\left|\vec{AE}\times\vec{AF}\right|$, and $\vec{AE}\times\vec{AF}=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-2&0&-6\\3&1&-1\end{matrix}\right|=6\hat i-20\hat j-2\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $ABDE$ and $ABCF$ are parallelograms, $\vec{AE}=\vec{BD}$ and $\vec{AF}=\vec{BC}$, so $\triangle AEF$ has the same area as $\triangle BCD$.
solution: In parallelogram $ABDE$ (vertices in order), $\vec{AE}=\vec{BD}$; in parallelogram $ABCF$, $\vec{AF}=\vec{BC}$.
Hence $\text{Area}(\triangle AEF)=\frac12\left|\vec{BD}\times\vec{BC}\right|=\text{Area}(\triangle BDC)$; no need to find $E$ or $F$.

useful_results: If $PQRS$ is a parallelogram (vertices in order) then $S=P+R-Q$, $\vec{PS}=\vec{QR}$ and the diagonals bisect each other: midpoint of $PR$ = midpoint of $QS$.
Area of the triangle with vertices $P,Q,R$ is $\frac12\left|\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}\right|$, valid in 3D; it depends only on the two edge vectors, so a translate of a triangle has the same area.
Translation-invariance: if $\vec{AE}=\vec{BD}$ and $\vec{AF}=\vec{BC}$, then $\triangle AEF$ is a translate of $\triangle BDC$ (translate $B\to A$), hence congruent. Here both areas are $\sqrt{110}$.

concepts: Volume of a tetrahedron (scalar triple product / Gram determinant) and shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the volume of a regular tetrahedron of edge length $k$ is $V$ and the shortest distance between any pair of opposite edges of the same regular tetrahedron is $d$, then find the value of $\frac{d^3}{V}$.
questions.key_idea: Both $V$ and $d$ come from the three edge vectors at one vertex, which have equal lengths $k$ and mutual angles $60^\circ$.
solution: Take vertex $O$ and edges $\vec{OA}=\vec a$, $\vec{OB}=\vec b$, $\vec{OC}=\vec c$ with $\left|\vec a\right|=\left|\vec b\right|=\left|\vec c\right|=k$ and all angles $60^\circ$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec c\cdot\vec a=\frac{k^2}{2}$; $V=\frac16\left|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\right|$.

$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\left|\begin{matrix}\vec a\cdot\vec a&\vec a\cdot\vec b&\vec a\cdot\vec c\\ \vec b\cdot\vec a&\vec b\cdot\vec b&\vec b\cdot\vec c\\ \vec c\cdot\vec a&\vec c\cdot\vec b&\vec c\cdot\vec c\end{matrix}\right|=k^6\left|\begin{matrix}1&\frac12&\frac12\\ \frac12&1&\frac12\\ \frac12&\frac12&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac{k^6}{2}$.
Shortest distance between opposite edges $OA$ and $BC$: $d=\frac{\left|(\vec b-\vec a)\cdot\left(\vec a\times(\vec c-\vec b)\right)\right|}{\left|\vec a\times(\vec c-\vec b)\right|}$.
The numerator reduces to $\left|\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)\right|=\left|[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec b]\right|=\frac{k^3}{\sqrt2}$ (the other terms contain a repeated vector).

$\left|\vec a\times(\vec c-\vec b)\right|^2=\left|\vec a\right|^2\left|\vec c-\vec b\right|^2-\left(\vec a\cdot(\vec c-\vec b)\right)^2$; here $\left|\vec c-\vec b\right|^2=k^2+k^2-2\cdot\frac{k^2}{2}=k^2$ and $\vec a\cdot(\vec c-\vec b)=\frac{k^2}2-\frac{k^2}2=0$.
So $\left|\vec a\times(\vec c-\vec b)\right|^2=k^4$ and $\left|\vec a\times(\vec c-\vec b)\right|=k^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Inscribe the regular tetrahedron in a cube of side $s$: its edges are face diagonals ($k=s\sqrt2$), $V=\frac{s^3}{3}$ and opposite edges lie on opposite faces, so $d=s$.
solution: Take the cube $[0,s]^3$ and the tetrahedron with vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(s,s,0)$, $(s,0,s)$, $(0,s,s)$; all six edges are face diagonals of length $s\sqrt2=k$.
Volume: the cube minus four corner pyramids, each $\frac13\cdot\frac{s^2}{2}\cdot s=\frac{s^3}{6}$, so $V=s^3-\frac{4s^3}{6}=\frac{s^3}{3}$.

Opposite edges, such as $(0,0,0)\!-\!(s,s,0)$ in the plane $z=0$ and $(s,0,s)\!-\!(0,s,s)$ in the plane $z=s$, lie in parallel faces and are perpendicular in projection, so the shortest distance between them is the distance between the planes: $d=s$.
$\frac{d^3}{V}=\frac{s^3}{s^3/3}=3$. (Check: $d=s=\frac{k}{\sqrt2}$ and $V=\frac{k^3}{6\sqrt2}$, as in the first method.)

useful_results: Regular tetrahedron of edge $k$: $V=\frac{k^3}{6\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}k^3$, shortest distance between opposite edges $d=\frac{k}{\sqrt2}$, height $\sqrt{\frac23}\,k$, circumradius $\frac{\sqrt6}{4}k$, inradius $\frac{\sqrt6}{12}k$.
A regular tetrahedron fits in a cube of side $\frac{k}{\sqrt2}$ using four alternate vertices; its volume is exactly one third of the cube's volume.
Gram determinant: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\det\left(\vec u_i\cdot\vec u_j\right)$, so volumes follow from lengths and angles alone, with no coordinates needed.
For any tetrahedron, $d(AB,CD)=\frac{6V}{\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}\right|}$; in the regular case $\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}\right|=k^2$ gives $d=\frac{6V}{k^2}=\frac{k}{\sqrt2}$.

concepts: Vector triple product and dot product of vectors
Maximum value of $\sin\alpha$ (trigonometric equation)
questions.question: Find the scalars $\alpha$ and $\beta$ if $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{b}=(4-2\beta-\sin\alpha)\vec{b}+(\beta^2-1)\vec{c}$ and $(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}=\vec{c}$, while $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are non-zero, non-collinear vectors.
questions.key_idea: Expand $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)$ and compare coefficients of the independent vectors $\vec b,\vec c$; then $\sin\alpha=(\beta-1)^2+1\le1$.
solution: Expand: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{b}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})$, so the left side is $\vec{b}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}+\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})$.
$\vec b,\vec c$ are non-collinear, hence independent, so coefficients can be compared with $(4-2\beta-\sin\alpha)\vec{b}+(\beta^2-1)\vec{c}$.
From $(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}=\vec{c}$, dot with $\vec c$: $(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c})(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}$, and $\vec c\neq\vec 0$, so $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=1$ ...(3).
Since $\sin\alpha\le1$ and $(\beta-1)^2+1\ge1$, both sides equal $1$: $\beta=1$ and $\sin\alpha=1$.
useful_results: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{b}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})$ (BAC-CAB); if $\vec b,\vec c$ are non-collinear, $\lambda\vec b+\mu\vec c=\vec 0$ forces $\lambda=\mu=0$.
$(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}=\vec{c}$ means $\vec a=\frac{\vec c}{|\vec c|^2}$ (for $\vec c\neq\vec0$), so $\vec a\cdot\vec c=1$ and $\vec a\parallel\vec c$.
A quadratic bounded by a trig value: $x^2-2x+2=(x-1)^2+1\ge1$, so $\sin\theta=x^2-2x+2$ (or $\cos\theta=\ldots$) forces $x=1$ and $\sin\theta=1$.
$\sin\alpha=1\iff\alpha=2m\pi+\frac{\pi}{2}$, which is the same family as $n\pi+(-1)^n\frac{\pi}{2}$.

concepts: Vector triple product and scalar triple product (coplanarity)
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\alpha\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\alpha\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. Find the value(s) of $\alpha$, if any, such that $\{(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\}\times(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})=\vec{0}$. Find the vector product when $\alpha=0$.
questions.answer: $\alpha=\frac{2}{3}$ only; for $\alpha=0$ the vector product is $-60\left(2\hat{i}+\hat{k}\right)$
questions.key_idea: $X\times Y=\vec0$ means $X=\vec0$, $Y=\vec0$ or $X\parallel Y$; every case forces $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.
solution: $\vec{a}=\langle\alpha,2,-3\rangle$, $\vec{b}=\langle1,2\alpha,-2\rangle$, $\vec{c}=\langle2,-\alpha,1\rangle$. Put $\vec X=(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec b\times\vec c)$; the condition is $\vec X\times(\vec c\times\vec a)=\vec 0$.
A cross product is zero only if one factor is zero or the two are parallel, so the cases are: I $\vec X=\lambda(\vec c\times\vec a)$, II $\vec c\times\vec a=\vec0$, III $\vec X=\vec0$.

Case I: dot $\vec X=\lambda(\vec c\times\vec a)$ with $\vec b$. Since $\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec a(\vec b\cdot\vec b)-\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$, we get $\vec b\cdot\vec X=(\vec b\cdot\vec b)[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)[\vec b\ \vec b\ \vec c]=|\vec b|^2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
The right side is $\lambda[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$, so $(|\vec b|^2-\lambda)[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.

If $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\neq0$ then $\lambda=|\vec b|^2$, which would make $\vec c\times\vec a\parallel\vec b$, i.e. $\vec b\perp\vec a$ and $\vec b\perp\vec c$. But $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-2\alpha^2$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=5\alpha+6$ are never both $0$. So $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.
Case II: $\vec c\times\vec a=\vec0$ needs $\vec c=k\vec a$: $2=k\alpha$, $-\alpha=2k$, $1=-3k$ give $k=-\frac13$, $\alpha=-6$ but then $-\alpha=6\neq2k$: not possible.
Case III: $\vec X=\vec0$ means $\vec a\times\vec b=\lambda(\vec b\times\vec c)$; dot with $\vec c$: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$, again $\alpha=\frac23$.

For $\alpha=0$: $\vec a=\langle0,2,-3\rangle$, $\vec b=\langle1,0,-2\rangle$, $\vec c=\langle2,0,1\rangle$. Then $\vec a\times\vec b=\langle-4,-3,-2\rangle$ and $\vec b\times\vec c=\langle0,-5,0\rangle$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's Case I stops at '[a b c]=0' after dotting with b, but that step gives (|b|^2 - lambda)[a b c] = 0, so the branch lambda=|b|^2 had to be excluded (done above: b.c=-2 alpha^2, a.b=5 alpha+6 never vanish together). The PDF also never worked out the second part (vector product at alpha=0); it is added here (answer -60(2i+k), verified by computer algebra). The alpha=2/3 answer itself is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\,\vec b$ to collapse the whole expression at once.
solution: With $\vec u=\vec a\times\vec b$: $\vec u\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec u\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec u\cdot\vec b)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\,\vec b$, because $\vec u\cdot\vec b=0$.
Therefore the given product is $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\,\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\{\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)-\vec a(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\}$.
$\vec a$ and $\vec c$ are never parallel for real $\alpha$ (that needs $\alpha^2=-4$), so $\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)-\vec a(\vec b\cdot\vec c)=\vec0$ only if $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0=\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
Here $\vec a\cdot\vec b=5\alpha+6$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-2\alpha^2$ cannot both vanish, so we need $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.
At $\alpha=0$: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=-10$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=6$, $\vec b\cdot\vec c=0$.

useful_results: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\,\vec b$, and more generally $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec c\times\vec d)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]\,\vec c-[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\,\vec d$.
The cross product of two vectors is $\vec0$ iff one is $\vec0$ or they are parallel; this splits a vector equation into a few clean cases.
$\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$; $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$ iff $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar.
Here: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=15\alpha-10$, so the three vectors are coplanar exactly when $\alpha=\frac23$.

concepts: Dot product of vectors and angle between vectors
Linear combination of vectors
questions.question: The figure shows non-zero vectors $\vec{v}$, $\vec{w}$ and $\vec{z}$, where $\vec z$ is orthogonal to the line $L$, and $\vec v$ and $\vec w$ make equal angles $\beta$ with the line $L$ ($\vec v$ comes in from the lower left towards the point on $L$, $\vec w$ goes out to the lower right, and $\vec z$ points straight down). Assuming $|\vec{v}|=|\vec{w}|$, if $\vec{w}$ is expressed as a linear combination of $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{z}$ as $\vec{w}=x\vec{v}+y\vec{z}$, find $x$ and $y$.
questions.key_idea: Dot $\vec w=x\vec v+y\vec z$ with $\vec v$ and with $\vec w$; the angle between $\vec v$ and $\vec z$ is $90^\circ+\beta$ and between $\vec w$ and $\vec z$ is $90^\circ-\beta$.
solution: $\vec{w}=x\vec{v}+y\vec{z}$ and $|\vec v|=|\vec w|$. Angles: $\vec v,\vec w$ make $2\beta$ with each other; $\vec v,\vec z$ make $90^\circ+\beta$; $\vec w,\vec z$ make $90^\circ-\beta$.
Dot with $\vec v$: $\vec w\cdot\vec v=x|\vec v|^2+y\,\vec z\cdot\vec v$.
Divide by $|\vec v|$ and use $|\vec v|=|\vec w|$: $|\vec w|\cos2\beta=x|\vec w|-y|\vec z|\sin\beta$ ...(1).
Dot $\vec w=x\vec v+y\vec z$ with $\vec w$: $|\vec w|^2=x|\vec v||\vec w|\cos2\beta+y|\vec z||\vec w|\cos(90^\circ-\beta)$.
Divide by $|\vec w|$: $|\vec w|=x|\vec w|\cos2\beta+y|\vec z|\sin\beta$ ...(2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Place $L$ along the $x$-axis and write the three vectors in components; compare the $x$- and $y$-components.
solution: Take $L$ as the $x$-axis. Then $\vec z=|\vec z|(0,-1)$, $\vec v=|\vec v|(\cos\beta,\sin\beta)$ (rising to $L$) and $\vec w=|\vec v|(\cos\beta,-\sin\beta)$ (falling from $L$), using $|\vec w|=|\vec v|$.
$\vec w=x\vec v+y\vec z$ in components: $x$-component $|\vec v|\cos\beta=x|\vec v|\cos\beta$.
Since $\cos\beta\neq0$ (the vector is not perpendicular to $L$ in the figure), $x=1$.
With $x=1$: $y|\vec z|=2|\vec v|\sin\beta$, so $y=\frac{2|\vec v|\sin\beta}{|\vec z|}$.

useful_results: Reflection (mirror) formula: the reflection of $\vec v$ in a surface with unit normal $\hat n$ is $\vec v-2(\vec v\cdot\hat n)\hat n$; here $\vec w=\vec v+\frac{2|\vec v|\sin\beta}{|\vec z|}\vec z$ is exactly that with $\hat n=\frac{\vec z}{|\vec z|}$.
To find coefficients in $\vec w=x\vec v+y\vec z$ without coordinates, dot with $\vec v$ and with $\vec w$ (or with any two convenient vectors) to get two linear equations.
Angle bookkeeping: if $\vec z\perp L$ and $\vec v$ makes $\beta$ with $L$, then $\vec v$ makes $90^\circ\mp\beta$ with $\vec z$, so $\vec v\cdot\vec z=\mp|\vec v||\vec z|\sin\beta$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and linear independence of vectors
Coplanarity of points
questions.question: Consider the non-zero vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{d}$ such that no three of them are coplanar. Prove that $\vec{a}\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec{c}\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]=\vec{b}\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec{d}\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]$. Hence prove that if $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are the position vectors of the vertices of a plane quadrilateral, then $\frac{\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]}{\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]}=1$.
questions.answer: Both statements are proved (the ratio equals $1$).
questions.key_idea: $\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ form a basis, so $\vec a=x\vec b+y\vec c+z\vec d$ with $x,y,z$ read off by triple products; plane points give a vanishing volume.
solution: No three of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are coplanar, so $\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are non-coplanar and $\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]\neq0$. Hence $\vec{a}=x\vec{b}+y\vec{c}+z\vec{d}$ for some scalars $x,y,z$.
Take the triple product with $\vec c,\vec d$: $\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]=x\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]$, since $\vec c$ and $\vec d$ repeated give $0$.
With $\vec b,\vec d$ in the other slots: $\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]=y\left[\vec{c}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]=-y\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]$.

Multiply $\vec a=x\vec b+y\vec c+z\vec d$ by $\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]$: $\vec a\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]=\vec b\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]-\vec c\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec d\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]$.

Rearranged: $\vec a\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec c\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]=\vec b\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec d\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]$. This proves the first part.

(2) If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are vertices of a plane quadrilateral, the vectors $\vec a-\vec b$, $\vec b-\vec c$, $\vec c-\vec d$ lie in that plane, so $[(\vec a-\vec b)\times(\vec b-\vec c)]\cdot(\vec c-\vec d)=0$.
$(\vec a-\vec b)\times(\vec b-\vec c)=\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c$ (as $\vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0$).

Dot with $\vec c-\vec d$ (terms with a repeated vector vanish): $\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]-\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]-\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]=0$.
questions.correction_note: Part (1): the PDF's printed lines are garbled (e.g. '[b c d](a - y c) = [b c d][x b + z d]', missing brackets and a stray '+c'); the logic (expand a in b, c, d and read the coefficients off with triple products) is right and has been rewritten cleanly with the same steps. Part (2): the PDF ends with the reciprocal form ([abc]+[acd])/([abd]+[bcd])=1, which is the same equation; it is restated in the form asked.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use a determinant: expanding a $4\times4$ determinant with a repeated column (or a column of ones) gives both identities.
solution: Consider the $4\times4$ determinant whose rows are $(a_i,a_1,a_2,a_3)$, $(b_i,b_1,b_2,b_3)$, $(c_i,c_1,c_2,c_3)$, $(d_i,d_1,d_2,d_3)$, for $i=1,2,3$. Two of its columns are equal, so it is $0$.

Expand along the first column: $a_i\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]-b_i\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+c_i\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]-d_i\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]=0$, for $i=1,2,3$.

Combining the three components: $\vec a\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]-\vec b\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\vec c\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]-\vec d\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]=\vec0$, which rearranges to the required identity.
For (2): four points are coplanar iff the determinant with rows $(1,\vec a),(1,\vec b),(1,\vec c),(1,\vec d)$ vanishes (the volume of the tetrahedron they span is $0$).
Expand along the column of ones: $\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]-\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]-\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]=0$.

Thus $\left[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}\right]=\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}\right]+\left[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\right]$, and the ratio is $1$ (denominator non-zero).

useful_results: For any four vectors in space: $\vec a[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]-\vec b[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec d]+\vec c[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]-\vec d[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec0$.
Four points with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are coplanar iff $[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]-[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec d]+[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]-[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.

If $\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are non-coplanar, the coefficients of $\vec a=x\vec b+y\vec c+z\vec d$ are $x=\frac{[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec d]}{[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]}$, $y=\frac{[\vec b\ \vec a\ \vec d]}{[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]}$, $z=\frac{[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]}{[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]}$ (Cramer's rule).
Triple products vanish whenever two vectors are equal, which is why dotting with a suitable cross product isolates one coefficient.

concepts: Cross product of vectors
Linear combination of non-coplanar vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{A}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{B}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, $\vec{C}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. If the vector $\vec{B}\times\vec{C}$ can be expressed as a linear combination $\vec{B}\times\vec{C}=x\vec{A}+y\vec{B}+z\vec{C}$, where $x,y,z$ are scalars, find the value of $100x+10y+8z$.
questions.key_idea: Compute $\vec B\times\vec C=2(1,-1,1)$, then match components to get three linear equations in $x,y,z$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Dot both sides with the reciprocal vectors $\vec B\times\vec C$, $\vec C\times\vec A$, $\vec A\times\vec B$ to isolate $x,y,z$ one at a time.
solution: $[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]=\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)=(1,-2,3)\cdot(2,-2,2)=12\neq0$, so $\vec A,\vec B,\vec C$ are a basis.
Dot $\vec B\times\vec C=x\vec A+y\vec B+z\vec C$ with $\vec B\times\vec C$: $|\vec B\times\vec C|^2=x[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]$, so $x=\frac{12}{12}=1$.

Dot with $\vec C\times\vec A$: $(\vec B\times\vec C)\cdot(\vec C\times\vec A)=(\vec B\cdot\vec C)(\vec C\cdot\vec A)-(\vec B\cdot\vec A)(\vec C\cdot\vec C)=0-(-3)(2)=6=y[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]$, so $y=\frac12$.

Dot with $\vec A\times\vec B$: $(\vec B\times\vec C)\cdot(\vec A\times\vec B)=(\vec B\cdot\vec A)(\vec C\cdot\vec B)-(\vec B\cdot\vec B)(\vec C\cdot\vec A)=0-6\cdot1=-6=z[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]$, so $z=-\frac12$.

useful_results: If $[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]\neq0$, any vector $\vec V=\frac{(\vec V\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C))\vec A+(\vec V\cdot(\vec C\times\vec A))\vec B+(\vec V\cdot(\vec A\times\vec B))\vec C}{[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]}$.
Lagrange's identity: $(\vec p\times\vec q)\cdot(\vec r\times\vec s)=(\vec p\cdot\vec r)(\vec q\cdot\vec s)-(\vec p\cdot\vec s)(\vec q\cdot\vec r)$.
A linear combination of three vectors exists for every target only when they are non-coplanar ($[\vec A\ \vec B\ \vec C]\neq0$); here it is $12$.

concepts: Linear combination of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{b}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{c}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the numbers $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ such that $\alpha\vec{a}+\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-5\\6\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.key_idea: Equating components turns the vector equation into a $3\times3$ linear system.
solution: Equate the three components of $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c$ with $(-2,-5,6)$.
From the second and third: $\beta=\gamma-5$ and $\alpha=\frac{\gamma-6}{3}$.
Substitute in the first: $\frac{\gamma-6}{3}+2\gamma-10+\gamma=-2$, so $\gamma-6+9\gamma-30=-6$, giving $10\gamma=30$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cramer's rule in triple-product form: $\alpha=\frac{[\vec r\ \vec b\ \vec c]}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]}$ and similarly for $\beta,\gamma$.
solution: $\alpha=\frac{[\vec r\ \vec b\ \vec c]}{10}$, with $[\vec r\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\left|\begin{matrix}-2&2&1\\-5&1&-1\\6&0&1\end{matrix}\right|=-2(1)-2(1)+1(-6)=-10$, so $\alpha=-1$.

useful_results: A vector equation $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec r$ has a unique solution iff $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\neq0$ (here $10$), and then $\alpha=\frac{[\vec r\ \vec b\ \vec c]}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]}$ etc.
Always substitute back into all three component equations to catch arithmetic slips.

concepts: Vector equation: dot and cross product identities
questions.question: Let a three-dimensional vector $\vec{V}$ satisfy $2\vec{V}+\vec{V}\times(\hat{i}+2\hat{j})=2\hat{i}+\hat{k}$. If $3|\vec{V}|=\sqrt{m}$ where $m\in\mathbb{N}$, find $m$.
questions.key_idea: Dot with $\hat i+2\hat j$ to get $\vec V\cdot(\hat i+2\hat j)=1$, then take the squared magnitude of both sides.
solution: Let $\vec u=\hat i+2\hat j$, so $2\vec V+\vec V\times\vec u=2\hat i+\hat k$ and $3|\vec V|=\sqrt m$.
Dot with $\vec u$: $2\vec V\cdot\vec u+(\vec V\times\vec u)\cdot\vec u=2\hat i\cdot\vec u+\hat k\cdot\vec u$, i.e. $2\vec V\cdot\vec u=2$, so $\vec V\cdot\vec u=1$.
Take squared magnitudes: $|2\vec V+\vec V\times\vec u|^2=|2\hat i+\hat k|^2=5$.
Expand: $4|\vec V|^2+|\vec V\times\vec u|^2+4\vec V\cdot(\vec V\times\vec u)=5$, and $\vec V\cdot(\vec V\times\vec u)=0$.
$|\vec V\times\vec u|^2=\vec V\cdot(\vec u\times(\vec V\times\vec u))=\vec V\cdot\left(\vec V|\vec u|^2-\vec u(\vec u\cdot\vec V)\right)=5|\vec V|^2-(\vec V\cdot\vec u)^2$.
So $4|\vec V|^2+5|\vec V|^2-1=5$ (using $\vec V\cdot\vec u=1$, $|\vec u|^2=5$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec V=(p,q,r)$, solve the resulting $3\times3$ linear system and compute $|\vec V|$ directly.
solution: The equation $2\vec V+\vec V\times\vec u=(2,0,1)$ gives $2p-2r=2$, $2q+r=0$, $2r+2p-q=1$.
From the first two: $p=1+r$, $q=-\frac r2$. Substitute in the third: $2r+2+2r+\frac r2=1$, so $\frac92r=-1$, $r=-\frac29$.

useful_results: For $\vec u$ fixed: $(\vec V\times\vec u)\cdot\vec u=0$ and $\vec V\cdot(\vec V\times\vec u)=0$, so dotting with $\vec u$ and squaring both sides removes the cross product.
$|\vec V\times\vec u|^2=|\vec V|^2|\vec u|^2-(\vec V\cdot\vec u)^2$ (Lagrange's identity).

The equation $k\vec V+\vec V\times\vec u=\vec w$ ($k\neq0$) has the unique solution $\vec V=\frac{k^2\vec w+(\vec u\cdot\vec w)\vec u+k\,\vec u\times\vec w}{k(k^2+|\vec u|^2)}$; here this gives $\vec V=\frac19(7,1,-2)$.

concepts: Linear independence and coplanarity of vectors
Polynomial identity (roots of a quadratic)
questions.question: If $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ are two non-zero and non-collinear vectors satisfying $[(a-2)\alpha^2+(b-3)\alpha+c]\vec{x}+[(a-2)\beta^2+(b-3)\beta+c]\vec{y}+[(a-2)\gamma^2+(b-3)\gamma+c](\vec{x}\times\vec{y})=\vec{0}$, where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are three distinct real numbers, then find the value of $a^2+b^2+c^2$.
questions.key_idea: $\vec x,\vec y,\vec x\times\vec y$ are independent, so each bracket is $0$: a quadratic with three distinct roots is identically $0$.
solution: $\vec x,\vec y$ are non-collinear, so $\vec x,\vec y,\vec x\times\vec y$ are non-coplanar, hence linearly independent.
Therefore each coefficient is zero: $(a-2)\alpha^2+(b-3)\alpha+c=0$, $(a-2)\beta^2+(b-3)\beta+c=0$ and $(a-2)\gamma^2+(b-3)\gamma+c=0$.
So the equation $(a-2)t^2+(b-3)t+c=0$ is satisfied by three distinct values $t=\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.
A quadratic with three distinct roots is an identity: all coefficients vanish.
useful_results: For non-collinear $\vec x,\vec y$, the vectors $\vec x,\vec y,\vec x\times\vec y$ are independent: dotting $p\vec x+q\vec y+r(\vec x\times\vec y)=\vec0$ with $\vec x\times\vec y$ gives $r=0$, then $p=q=0$.
A polynomial of degree at most $n$ with more than $n$ distinct roots is the zero polynomial; the same follows from the non-zero Vandermonde determinant $(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)$.
Recognition cue: a coefficient pattern $f(\alpha),f(\beta),f(\gamma)$ with the same $f$ points to a polynomial-roots argument.

concepts: Parallelogram: sides and area using vectors (cross product)
questions.question: The diagonals of a parallelogram are given by the vectors $2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-\hat{k}$. Determine its sides and also the area.
questions.answer: Sides $\frac12\left(5\hat i-\hat j-7\hat k\right)$ and $\frac12\left(-\hat i+7\hat j-5\hat k\right)$; area $\frac12\sqrt{1274}$ sq. units
questions.key_idea: If $\vec a,\vec b$ are the sides then $\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec a-\vec b$ are the diagonals, and area $=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$.
solution: Let $\vec a,\vec b$ be adjacent sides. Then $\vec a+\vec b=(2,3,-6)=\vec d_1$ and $\vec a-\vec b=(3,-4,-1)=\vec d_2$.
Area $=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ (the diagonals split the parallelogram into four triangles).
$\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&3&-6\\3&-4&-1\end{matrix}\right|$ $=\hat i(-3-24)-\hat j(-2+18)+\hat k(-8-9)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the second diagonal as a-b=(3,4,-1) (sign slip) although it then uses the correct (3,-4,-1) to get a and b; it also writes 'Area = d1 x d2' and shows the factor 1/2 only in the next line. Corrected to a-b=(3,-4,-1) and Area = (1/2)|d1 x d2|. The sides and the area (1/2)sqrt(1274) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: The diagonals are perpendicular, so the parallelogram is a rhombus and its area is half the product of the diagonals.
solution: $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=6-12+6=0$, so the diagonals are perpendicular.
A parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus, so $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$.
Each side has length $\frac12\sqrt{|\vec d_1|^2+|\vec d_2|^2}=\frac12\sqrt{75}=\frac{5\sqrt3}{2}$, matching $|\vec a|^2=\frac{25+1+49}{4}$ for $\vec a=\frac12(5,-1,-7)$.
The side vectors themselves are $\frac{\vec d_1\pm\vec d_2}{2}$, as before.

useful_results: Sides $\vec a,\vec b$ and diagonals $\vec d_1=\vec a+\vec b$, $\vec d_2=\vec a-\vec b$: $\vec a=\frac{\vec d_1+\vec d_2}{2}$, $\vec b=\frac{\vec d_1-\vec d_2}{2}$, area $=|\vec a\times\vec b|=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$.
Parallelogram law: $|\vec d_1|^2+|\vec d_2|^2=2(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2)$; here $49+26=75=2\cdot\frac{75}{2}$.
Diagonals perpendicular ($\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=0$) iff $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$ (rhombus); then area $=\frac12|\vec d_1||\vec d_2|$.

concepts: Homogeneous linear system and determinants (non-trivial solution)
questions.question: Find the value of $\lambda$ such that $a,b,c$ are all non-zero and $(-4\hat{i}+5\hat{j})a+(3\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+\hat{k})b+(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k})c=\lambda(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k})$.
questions.key_idea: Equating components gives a homogeneous system in $a,b,c$; a non-zero solution needs its determinant to vanish.
solution: A homogeneous system has a non-zero solution only if $\left|\begin{matrix}-4-\lambda&3&1\\5&-3-\lambda&1\\0&1&3-\lambda\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
Non-zero check: from (iii) $b=(\lambda-3)c$; $\lambda=0$ gives $(a,b,c)\propto(-2,-3,1)$; $\lambda=-2\pm\sqrt{29}$ gives $\left(\frac{15-4\lambda}{5},\lambda-3,1\right)$, all non-zero.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's determinant expansion contains arithmetic slips: it writes '(4+lambda)(9-lambda^2+1)-5(8-lambda)' (should be '5(8-3 lambda)' and (lambda^2-10)), reaches 'lambda^3+4 lambda^2+15 lambda=0', then 'lambda^2+4 lambda-15=0' and 'lambda=-4 +- sqrt(29)', which are inconsistent with each other. The correct determinant is -lambda(lambda^2+4 lambda-25), giving lambda=0, -2 +- sqrt(29) (which is what the printed answer says). A final check that a,b,c are non-zero is added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate instead of using a determinant: scale $c=1$, express $b$ then $a$ in $\lambda$ from (iii) and (ii), and substitute in (i).
solution: If $c=0$ then (iii) gives $b=0$ and (ii) gives $a=0$; so $c\neq0$ and by homogeneity take $c=1$.

Check that $a,b$ are non-zero: $b=\lambda-3
eq0$ for these values, and $a= rac{\lambda^2-10}{5}= rac{15-4\lambda}{5}
eq0$ since $\lambda
eq rac{15}{4}$ (using $\lambda^2=25-4\lambda$ for the roots of the quadratic; for $\lambda=0$, $a=-2$).

useful_results: The equation $M\vec x=\lambda\vec x$ has a non-zero solution iff $\det(M-\lambda I)=0$: $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the matrix of coefficients, here $M=\begin{pmatrix}-4&3&1\\5&-3&1\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}$.

For a $3\times3$ matrix, $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda^3-(\mathrm{tr}M)\lambda^2+(\text{sum of principal }2\times2\text{ minors})\lambda-\det M$; here $\mathrm{tr}M=-4$, minors sum $-25$, $\det M=0$, giving $\lambda^3+4\lambda^2-25\lambda$.
Sum of the roots $0+(-2+\sqrt{29})+(-2-\sqrt{29})=-4=\mathrm{tr}M$: a quick check on the cubic.

concepts: Cross product (vector perpendicular to two vectors)
Plane and dot product condition
questions.question: Find the vector $\vec{r}$ which is perpendicular to $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}\cdot\left(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}\right)+8=0$.
questions.key_idea: A vector perpendicular to both is $\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$; the dot-product condition fixes $\lambda$.
solution: $\vec r\perp\vec a$ and $\vec r\perp\vec b$, so $\vec r=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-2&5\\2&3&-1\end{matrix}\right|=-13\hat i+11\hat j+7\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec r=(x,y,z)$ and solve the three linear equations $\vec r\cdot\vec a=0$, $\vec r\cdot\vec b=0$, $\vec r\cdot(2,1,1)=-8$.

useful_results: The set of vectors perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors $\vec a,\vec b$ is the line $\{\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)\}$; one more linear condition (as here) picks a single vector.
If instead the extra condition is $|\vec r|=k$, then $\lambda=\pm\frac{k}{|\vec a\times\vec b|}$; here $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{169+121+49}=\sqrt{339}$.
Check: $\vec r\cdot\vec a=-13-22+35=0$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec b=-26+33-7=0$.

concepts: Orthocentre of a triangle using vectors (perpendicularity by dot product)
questions.question: Two vertices of a triangle are at $-\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$ and $2\hat{i}+5\hat{j}$ and its orthocentre is at $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$. Find the position vector of the third vertex.
questions.key_idea: The line from each known vertex to the orthocentre is perpendicular to the side through the third vertex: two dot-product equations.
solution: Direction of altitude from $Q$ (line $QH$): $\vec{QH}$ is along $(1,3)$. Direction of altitude from $P$ (line $PH$): along $(2,-1)$.
The altitude from $Q$ is perpendicular to $PC$: $(1,3)\cdot(\alpha+1,\beta-3)=0$.
The altitude from $P$ is perpendicular to $QC$: $(2,-1)\cdot(\alpha-2,\beta-5)=0$.
The third vertex is $\left(\frac57,\frac{17}{7}\right)$, i.e. $\frac57\hat i+\frac{17}{7}\hat j$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinate geometry with slopes: intersect the two lines through $P$ and $Q$ perpendicular to the altitudes $QH$ and $PH$.
solution: Slope of $QH$: $\frac{5-2}{2-1}=3$, so side $PC\perp QH$ has slope $-\frac13$: $y-3=-\frac13(x+1)$, i.e. $x+3y=8$.
Slope of $PH$: $\frac{3-2}{-1-1}=-\frac12$, so side $QC\perp PH$ has slope $2$: $y-5=2(x-2)$, i.e. $2x-y=-1$.
Solve $x+3y=8$ and $2x-y=-1$: from the second $y=2x+1$; then $x+6x+3=8$, so $x=\frac57$, $y=\frac{17}{7}$.

useful_results: Orthocentre $H$ condition: $(\vec A-\vec H)\cdot(\vec B-\vec C)=0$ for each vertex $A$ with opposite side $BC$; any two of the three conditions imply the third.

With circumcentre $O$ and centroid $G$: $\vec H=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C-2\vec O$ and $\vec H=3\vec G-2\vec O$ (Euler line); here $O=\left(\frac5{14},\frac{59}{14}\right)$ and the formula returns $(1,2)$.
The third condition acts as a free check: $\vec{CH}\cdot\vec{PQ}=0$ holds for the answer.

concepts: Parallel vectors and cross product
Intermediate value theorem
questions.question: Let $\vec{A}(t)=f_1(t)\hat{i}+f_2(t)\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}(t)=g_1(t)\hat{i}+g_2(t)\hat{j}$, $t\in[0,1]$, where $f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2$ are continuous functions. If $\vec{A}(t)$ and $\vec{B}(t)$ are nonzero vectors for all $t$ and $\vec{A}(0)=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$, $\vec{A}(1)=6\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$, $\vec{B}(0)=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$, $\vec{B}(1)=2\hat{i}+6\hat{j}$, then show that $\vec{A}(t)$ and $\vec{B}(t)$ are parallel for some $t$.
questions.key_idea: Parallel means $f_1g_2-f_2g_1=0$; this is a continuous function of $t$ whose values at $0$ and $1$ have opposite signs, so the intermediate value theorem applies.
solution: Two nonzero vectors $\vec{A}(t),\vec{B}(t)$ are parallel for some $t\in[0,1]$ if and only if $\frac{f_1(t)}{g_1(t)}=\frac{f_2(t)}{g_2(t)}$, i.e. $f_1(t)g_2(t)=f_2(t)g_1(t)$ for some $t\in[0,1]$.
Since $f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2$ are continuous, $h$ is continuous on $[0,1]$.
By the intermediate value theorem there is some $t\in(0,1)$ with $h(t)=0$.
For this $t$, $\vec{A}(t)$ and $\vec{B}(t)$ are parallel vectors.
useful_results: In the plane, nonzero $\vec{A}=(f_1,f_2)$ and $\vec{B}=(g_1,g_2)$ are parallel exactly when $f_1g_2-f_2g_1=0$ (the 2D cross product); this avoids dividing by a component that may be $0$.

Intermediate value theorem: if $h$ is continuous on $[p,q]$ and $h(p)h(q)<0$, then $h(t)=0$ for some $t\in(p,q)$. 'Show that something happens for some $t$' often means build a continuous $h$ and find a sign change.

The same idea gives: if a continuous nonzero vector $\vec{A}(t)$ turns from $\vec{B}(0)$'s side to the other side of $\vec{B}$, they must be parallel at some moment (sign change of the cross product).
Instance: with $h(t)=f_1g_2-f_2g_1$, the endpoints give $h(0)=2\cdot2-3\cdot3=-5$ and $h(1)=6\cdot6-2\cdot2=32$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and volume of a parallelepiped
AM-GM inequality
questions.question: Let $V$ be the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the vectors $\vec{a}=a_1\hat{i}+a_2\hat{j}+a_3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=b_1\hat{i}+b_2\hat{j}+b_3\hat{k}$, $\vec{c}=c_1\hat{i}+c_2\hat{j}+c_3\hat{k}$. If $a_r,b_r,c_r$, where $r=1,2,3$, are non-negative real numbers and $\sum_{r=1}^{3}\left(a_r+b_r+c_r\right)=3L$, show that $V\le L^3$.
questions.key_idea: Group the nine entries by columns: AM-GM on the three column sums gives $L^3\ge S_1S_2S_3$, and every term of the determinant appears (with plus sign) in that product.
solution: The volume is $V=\left|[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]\right|$, the modulus of the determinant with rows $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$, $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$, $(c_1,c_2,c_3)$.
Expanding $S_1S_2S_3$ gives $27$ terms: $a_1b_2c_3+a_2b_3c_1+a_3b_1c_2$ and $24$ more such terms, all $\ge0$ because $a_r,b_r,c_r\ge0$.
The product $S_1S_2S_3$ also contains the three terms of $N$ (and the rest are $\ge0$), so in the same way $L^3\ge N$.
Since $P,N\ge0$: $P-N\le P\le L^3$ and $N-P\le N\le L^3$, so $\left|P-N\right|\le L^3$.
questions.correction_note: PDF takes $V=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=P-N$ with no modulus and proves only $P-N\le L^3$. Volume is $|P-N|$, so the case $N-P\le N\le L^3$ is added (the PDF's own 'same reason' argument covers $N\le L^3$). Everything else is as printed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Hadamard: $V\le\prod$ (lengths of the column vectors) $\le S_1S_2S_3$, then AM-GM.
solution: The determinant of the matrix with rows $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ equals that of its transpose, so $V$ is also the volume of the parallelepiped with edge vectors the columns $C_j=(a_j,b_j,c_j)$.
A parallelepiped's volume is at most the product of its edge lengths (volume = base area $\times$ height, each factor at most the product of the lengths), so $V\le|C_1||C_2||C_3|$.
Because all entries are $\ge0$, $a_j^2+b_j^2+c_j^2\le\left(a_j+b_j+c_j\right)^2$ (the cross terms are non-negative), so $|C_j|\le S_j$.

useful_results: Hadamard's inequality: $\left|\det M\right|\le\prod_j\|C_j\|$ over the columns (or rows) of $M$; geometrically, a parallelepiped's volume is at most the product of its edge lengths, with equality for a rectangular box.
For non-negative entries, $\|C_j\|\le$ (sum of entries of $C_j$), since $\sum x_i^2\le\left(\sum x_i\right)^2$ when all $x_i\ge0$.
AM-GM: for $S_1,S_2,S_3\ge0$ with sum $3L$, $S_1S_2S_3\le L^3$, with equality iff $S_1=S_2=S_3$. Example: the identity matrix has $V=1$, $3L=3$, so $L=1$ and $V=L^3$.
The expansion of $\prod(a_j+b_j+c_j)$ contains every 'one entry from each column' product, hence all six determinant terms (3 positive, 3 negative) each with plus sign.

concepts: Angle bisector vector
Scalar and vector triple products
questions.question: If $\vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}$ are three non-coplanar unit vectors and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are the angles between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$, $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{w}$, $\vec{w}$ and $\vec{u}$ respectively and $\vec{x},\vec{y},\vec{z}$ are unit vectors along the bisectors of the angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ respectively. Prove that $\left[\vec{x}\times\vec{y}\ \ \vec{y}\times\vec{z}\ \ \vec{z}\times\vec{x}\right]=\frac{1}{16}\left[\vec{u}\ \vec{v}\ \vec{w}\right]^2\sec^2\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec^2\frac{\beta}{2}\sec^2\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
questions.key_idea: The diagonal $\vec u+\vec v$ of the rhombus on unit vectors $\vec u,\vec v$ bisects their angle and has length $2\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}$, so $\vec x=\frac{\vec u+\vec v}{2\cos(\alpha/2)}$; then use $[\vec x\times\vec y\ \vec y\times\vec z\ \vec z\times\vec x]=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]^2$.
solution: Take $\overrightarrow{OA}=\vec u$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\vec v$ and complete the parallelogram $OAPB$; as $|\vec u|=|\vec v|=1$ it is a rhombus, so $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB=\alpha$.
Hence $\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec u+\vec v$ lies along the bisector, so $\vec x=\frac{\vec u+\vec v}{\left|\vec u+\vec v\right|}$.
$\left|\vec u+\vec v\right|^2=1+1+2\vec u\cdot\vec v=2+2\cos\alpha=4\cos^2\frac{\alpha}{2}$, so $\left|\vec u+\vec v\right|=2\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}$.

Therefore $\vec x=\frac12\sec\frac{\alpha}{2}\left(\vec u+\vec v\right)$; similarly $\vec y=\frac12\sec\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\vec v+\vec w\right)$ and $\vec z=\frac12\sec\frac{\gamma}{2}\left(\vec w+\vec u\right)$.
$\left[\vec x\times\vec y\ \ \vec y\times\vec z\ \ \vec z\times\vec x\right]=\left(\vec x\times\vec y\right)\cdot\left[\left(\vec y\times\vec z\right)\times\left(\vec z\times\vec x\right)\right]$.

By the vector triple product, $\left(\vec y\times\vec z\right)\times\left(\vec z\times\vec x\right)=\left[\vec y\ \vec z\ \vec x\right]\vec z-\left[\vec y\ \vec z\ \vec z\right]\vec x=\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]\vec z$ (as $\left[\vec y\ \vec z\ \vec z\right]=0$).
So the expression is $\left(\vec x\times\vec y\right)\cdot\vec z\,\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]=\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]^2$ ...(i).
$\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]=\frac18\sec\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec\frac{\beta}{2}\sec\frac{\gamma}{2}\left[\vec u+\vec v\ \ \vec v+\vec w\ \ \vec w+\vec u\right]$.

Expanding $\left(\vec u+\vec v\right)\cdot\left[\left(\vec v+\vec w\right)\times\left(\vec w+\vec u\right)\right]$, every triple product with a repeated vector vanishes, leaving $\left[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w\right]+\left[\vec v\ \vec w\ \vec u\right]=2\left[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w\right]$.

So $\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]=\frac14\sec\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec\frac{\beta}{2}\sec\frac{\gamma}{2}\left[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w\right]$, and squaring, $\left[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z\right]^2=\frac1{16}\left[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w\right]^2\sec^2\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec^2\frac{\beta}{2}\sec^2\frac{\gamma}{2}$ ...(ii).
From (i) and (ii) the required result follows.
useful_results: For unit vectors $\vec u,\vec v$ at angle $\alpha<\pi$, $\vec u+\vec v$ bisects the angle and $\left|\vec u+\vec v\right|=2\cos\frac\alpha2$; for non-unit vectors the bisector direction is $\hat u+\hat v$.
$\left[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a\right]=\left[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c\right]^2$ for any three vectors.
$\left[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a\right]=2\left[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c\right]$.
A triple product with a repeated vector is $0$, and it is unchanged by cyclic permutation; use this to drop terms on expansion.

questions.question: $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ and $\vec d$ are the position vectors of the points $A(x,y,z)$, $B(y,-2z,3x)$, $C(2z,3x,-y)$ and $D(1,-1,2)$ respectively. If $\left|\vec a\right|=2\sqrt3$, the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ equals the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec c$, the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec d$ is $\frac{\pi}{2}$, and the angle between $\vec a$ and $\hat j$ is obtuse, then find $x,y,z$.
questions.key_idea: $\left|\vec b\right|=\left|\vec c\right|$ identically, so equal angles with $\vec a$ means $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec c$; together with $\vec a\cdot\vec d=0$ this reduces to a perfect square.
solution: $\vec a=(x,y,z)$, $\vec b=(y,-2z,3x)$, $\vec c=(2z,3x,-y)$, $\vec d=(1,-1,2)$ and $\left|\vec a\right|=2\sqrt3$.
The angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec d$ is $90^\circ$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec d=0$: $x-y+2z=0$ ...(i).
The angle between $\vec a$ and $\hat j$ is obtuse, so $\vec a\cdot\hat j=y<0$ (since $y=z$ later, the PDF states it as $z<0$).
$\left|\vec b\right|^2=y^2+4z^2+9x^2$ and $\left|\vec c\right|^2=4z^2+9x^2+y^2$, so $\left|\vec b\right|=\left|\vec c\right|$.

From $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec b\right|}=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec c\right|}$ we get $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec c$: $xy-2yz+3xz=2xz+3xy-yz$.
For $\vec a\cdot\hat j=y<0$ we need $y=z<0$, so $z=-2$, $y=-2$, $x=2$.
useful_results: If $\left|\vec b\right|=\left|\vec c\right|$, then $\vec a$ makes equal angles with $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ iff $\vec a\cdot\left(\vec b-\vec c\right)=0$.
The angle between $\vec a=(x,y,z)$ and $\hat j$ is obtuse iff $y<0$ (similarly for $\hat i,\hat k$ with $x,z$): use it to choose among sign-symmetric solutions.
A condition like $2x^2+4xz+2z^2=0$ is a perfect square, so it forces a linear relation rather than giving two roots; look for such squares after substituting a linear constraint.
Check for $(2,-2,-2)$: $\vec b=(-2,4,6)$ and $\vec c=(-4,6,2)$, both of length $\sqrt{56}$, and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec c=-24$, $\vec a\cdot\vec d=0$.

concepts: Dot product and orthogonal projection
questions.question: If $\vec r$ and $\vec s$ are nonzero constant vectors and the scalar $b$ is chosen such that $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|$ is minimum, then show that the value of $\left|b\vec s\right|^2+\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2$ is equal to $\left|\vec r\right|^2$.
questions.key_idea: At the minimum, $b=-\frac{\vec r\cdot\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}$, which makes $b\vec s$ cancel the cross term $2b\,\vec r\cdot\vec s$ exactly.
solution: Minimising $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|$ is the same as minimising $f(b)=\left|\vec r\right|^2+b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2+2b\,\vec r\cdot\vec s$ under the square root.

$f'(b)=\frac{2b\left|\vec s\right|^2+2\,\vec r\cdot\vec s}{2\sqrt{\left|\vec r\right|^2+b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2+2b\,\vec r\cdot\vec s}}$, which is zero when $2b\left|\vec s\right|^2+2\,\vec r\cdot\vec s=0$.
So $b=-\frac{\vec r\cdot\vec s}{\left|\vec s\right|^2}$ (it is a minimum: $f'$ changes sign from negative to positive there).
$\left|b\vec s\right|^2+\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2=b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2+\left|\vec r\right|^2+b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2+2b\,\vec r\cdot\vec s$.
Since $b\left|\vec s\right|^2=-\vec r\cdot\vec s$, we get $2b\,\vec r\cdot\vec s=-2b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2$.
So the value is $2b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2+\left|\vec r\right|^2-2b^2\left|\vec s\right|^2=\left|\vec r\right|^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The shortest $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|$ occurs at the perpendicular foot, so $\left(\vec r+b\vec s\right)\perp\vec s$ and Pythagoras gives the result.
solution: The points $\vec r+b\vec s$ ($b$ real) trace the straight line through $\vec r$ parallel to $\vec s$; $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|$ is the distance of its point from the origin.
This distance is least at the foot of the perpendicular from the origin, so $\left(\vec r+b\vec s\right)\cdot\vec s=0$ at the chosen $b$.
Hence $\vec r+b\vec s$ is perpendicular to $\vec s$, and therefore also perpendicular to $b\vec s$.
Write $\vec r=\left(\vec r+b\vec s\right)+\left(-b\vec s\right)$, a sum of two perpendicular vectors.
By Pythagoras, $\left|\vec r\right|^2=\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2+\left|-b\vec s\right|^2=\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2+\left|b\vec s\right|^2$, which is the required value.

useful_results: The scalar $b$ minimising $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|$ is $b=-\frac{\vec r\cdot\vec s}{\left|\vec s\right|^2}$; then $\vec r+b\vec s$ is the component of $\vec r$ perpendicular to $\vec s$ (and $-b\vec s$ is the projection of $\vec r$ on $\vec s$).
Minimum value: $\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2_{\min}=\left|\vec r\right|^2-\frac{(\vec r\cdot\vec s)^2}{\left|\vec s\right|^2}$ (valid for $\vec s\neq\vec 0$).
Pythagoras form: $\left|\vec r\right|^2=p^2+n^2$, with $p$ the length of the projection on $\vec s$ and $n$ the length of the perpendicular part, is the identity behind this question.
Example: $\vec r=(1,2,0)$, $\vec s=(1,0,0)$ gives $b=-1$, $\left|b\vec s\right|^2+\left|\vec r+b\vec s\right|^2=1+4=5=\left|\vec r\right|^2$.

concepts: Coplanar vectors and angle between vectors
questions.question: Given four nonzero vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ and $\vec d$. The vectors $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are coplanar but not collinear pair by pair, and vector $\vec d$ is not coplanar with $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$. If the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec a$ is $\alpha$ and the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec b$ is $\beta$, then prove that the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec c$ equals $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\right)$.
questions.key_idea: In the plane of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, write $\vec c=x\vec a+y\vec b$; dotting with $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ gives $\frac{x|\vec a|}{|\vec c|}=-1$ and $\frac{y|\vec b|}{|\vec c|}=1$, i.e. $\hat c=\hat b-\hat a$.
solution: Let the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec c$ be $\theta$. $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar and not collinear, so $\vec c=x\vec a+y\vec b$.
Dot with $\vec b$: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=x\,\vec a\cdot\vec b+y\left|\vec b\right|^2$ ...(a).

Dot with $\vec d$: $\vec d\cdot\vec c=x\,\vec d\cdot\vec a+y\,\vec d\cdot\vec b$, so $\left|\vec d\right|\left|\vec c\right|\cos\theta=x\left|\vec d\right|\left|\vec a\right|\cos\alpha+y\left|\vec d\right|\left|\vec b\right|\cos\beta$.
Divide by $\left|\vec d\right|\left|\vec c\right|$: $\cos\theta=x\frac{\left|\vec a\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}\cos\alpha+y\frac{\left|\vec b\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}\cos\beta$ ...(1).

Using (a) with $\left|\vec b\right|\left|\vec c\right|\cos\frac\pi3=x\left|\vec b\right|\left|\vec a\right|\cos\frac\pi3+y\left|\vec b\right|^2$ and dividing by $\left|\vec b\right|\left|\vec c\right|$: $\frac12=\frac{x}{2}\frac{\left|\vec a\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}+y\frac{\left|\vec b\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}$ ...(2).

Dot with $\vec c$: $\left|\vec c\right|^2=x\,\vec a\cdot\vec c+y\,\vec b\cdot\vec c$. The coplanar $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ have angle $\frac\pi3$ at each step on opposite sides of $\vec b$, so the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec c$ is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ (it cannot be $0$, as they are not collinear).

Hence $\left|\vec c\right|^2=x\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec c\right|\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}+y\left|\vec b\right|\left|\vec c\right|\cos\frac\pi3$, i.e. $2=-x\frac{\left|\vec a\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}+y\frac{\left|\vec b\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}$ ...(3).
Write $X=\frac{x\left|\vec a\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}$, $Y=\frac{y\left|\vec b\right|}{\left|\vec c\right|}$. (2) is $1=X+2Y$ and (3) is $2=-X+Y$. Adding: $3=3Y$, so $Y=1$ and $X=-1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Three unit vectors in a plane at $60^\circ$ steps satisfy $\hat a+\hat c=\hat b$ (rhombus), so $\hat d\cdot\hat c=\hat d\cdot\hat b-\hat d\cdot\hat a$.
solution: $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar, the angle between $\vec a,\vec b$ and between $\vec b,\vec c$ is $\frac\pi3$, and $\vec a,\vec c$ are not collinear, so $\hat a$ and $\hat c$ lie on opposite sides of $\hat b$ (same side would make them parallel).
Take axes in that plane with $\hat b=(1,0)$. Then $\hat a=\left(\cos60^\circ,-\sin60^\circ\right)$ and $\hat c=\left(\cos60^\circ,\sin60^\circ\right)$.
Adding, $\hat a+\hat c=\left(2\cos60^\circ,0\right)=(1,0)=\hat b$, so $\hat c=\hat b-\hat a$ (the rhombus with unit sides and a $120^\circ$ angle).
Dot with the unit vector $\hat d$: $\hat d\cdot\hat c=\hat d\cdot\hat b-\hat d\cdot\hat a$.
These dot products are $\cos\theta$, $\cos\beta$, $\cos\alpha$, so $\cos\theta=\cos\beta-\cos\alpha$, giving $\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\right)$.

useful_results: If $\hat a,\hat b,\hat c$ are coplanar unit vectors with $\hat b$ between $\hat a$ and $\hat c$, each at angle $\varphi$ from $\hat b$, then $\hat a+\hat c=2\cos\varphi\,\hat b$; for $\varphi=60^\circ$ this is $\hat a+\hat c=\hat b$.
For any vector $\vec d$: $\hat d\cdot\left(\hat a+\hat c\right)=2\cos\varphi\,\hat d\cdot\hat b$, so cosines of angles with coplanar vectors satisfy the same linear relation as the vectors.
Coplanarity of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ means $\vec c=x\vec a+y\vec b$; dotting with each vector gives a linear system for $x,y$.
Check ($\alpha=\beta$): then $\hat d\cdot\hat c=0$, i.e. $\vec d\perp\vec c$, consistent with $\cos\beta-\cos\alpha=0$.

Volume of a tetrahedron and altitude
questions.question: The position vectors of the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of a tetrahedron are $(1,1,1)$, $(1,0,0)$ and $(3,0,0)$ respectively. The altitude from the vertex $D$ to the opposite face $ABC$ meets the median line through $A$ of the triangle $ABC$ at a point $E$. If the length of side $AD$ is $4$ and the volume of the tetrahedron is $\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, then find all possible position vectors of the point $E$.
questions.key_idea: The volume fixes the height $DE=2$, so in the right triangle $ADE$, $AE^2=16-4=12$; $E$ is a point of line $AF$ at distance $2\sqrt3$ from $A$, on either side.
solution: $F$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $F=(2,0,0)=2\hat i$; the median through $A$ is the line $AF$.
$DE$ is the altitude to plane $ABC$ and $E$ lies in that plane, so $DE\perp AE$. Let $E$ divide $AF$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$.
$E=\frac{2\lambda\hat i+1\left(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\right)}{\lambda+1}=\frac{2\lambda+1}{\lambda+1}\hat i+\frac{1}{\lambda+1}\hat j+\frac{1}{\lambda+1}\hat k$.
Area of base $=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{BC}\times\overrightarrow{BA}\right|=\frac12\left|2\hat i\times\left(\hat j+\hat k\right)\right|=\sqrt2$.
Volume = one third of base area times height: $\frac13\sqrt2\cdot DE=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, so $DE=2$.
As $\angle AED$ is a right angle, $AD^2=AE^2+DE^2$, so $AE^2=16-4=12$.
For $\lambda=-2$: $E=\frac{-3\hat i+\hat j+\hat k}{-1}=3\hat i-\hat j-\hat k$.
For $\lambda=-\frac23$: $E=\frac{-\frac13\hat i+\hat j+\hat k}{\frac13}=-\hat i+3\hat j+3\hat k$.
So the possible positions of $E$ are $(-1,3,3)$ and $(3,-1,-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $D$ first with coordinates: height $2$ from plane $y=z$, foot on the median, and $AD=4$ give $E$ directly.
solution: $\overrightarrow{BC}=(2,0,0)$ and $\overrightarrow{BA}=(0,1,1)$, so a normal to plane $ABC$ is $(0,1,-1)$ and the plane is $y=z$ (it contains $A$, $B$, $C$).
Area of $ABC=\sqrt2$ and volume $\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}=\frac13\sqrt2\,h$ give height $h=2$, so $D=(p,q,r)$ has $\frac{\left|q-r\right|}{\sqrt2}=2$, i.e. $q-r=\pm2\sqrt2$.
The foot of the altitude is $E=D-\frac{q-r}{2}(0,1,-1)=\left(p,\frac{q+r}{2},\frac{q+r}{2}\right)$.
$E$ lies on line $AF$: points $(1+t,1-t,1-t)$, so $p-1=-\left(\frac{q+r}{2}-1\right)$. Put $m=\frac{q+r}{2}-1$, $s=\frac{q-r}{2}$ ($s^2=2$) and $p-1=-m$.
Both agree with the first method.

useful_results: Volume of a tetrahedron $=\frac13\times$ (base area) $\times$ (height), and also $\frac16\left|[\overrightarrow{AB}\ \overrightarrow{AC}\ \overrightarrow{AD}]\right|$. The altitude's foot $E$ lies in the base plane, so $\triangle ADE$ is right-angled at $E$.

A point on a given line at a given distance $\ell$ from a given point $A$ always has two solutions $A\pm\ell\hat u$; in ratio language this is the negative ratio, i.e. a point of the line outside the segment.
The median line through $A$ is the line through $A$ and the midpoint $F=\frac{\vec B+\vec C}{2}$ of $BC$; the problem says 'median line', so points beyond $A$ or $F$ are allowed.
